scenarios.title: Scenario 5 — Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenarios.domains: D3 Claude Code Configuration & Workflows · D4 Prompt Engineering & Structured Output
scenarios.brief: A fintech team runs Claude Code in GitHub Actions on about 240 pull requests a week. Three workloads: a blocking pre-merge review that posts inline comments and must finish within five minutes, on-demand test generation for uncovered branches, and a cost-sensitive nightly technical-debt sweep over about 2,400 files. The security team's dashboard consumes review findings in a fixed shape. CLAUDE.md and .claude/ are committed to the repository.

scenarios.title: Scenario 6 — Structured Data Extraction
scenarios.domains: D4 Prompt Engineering & Structured Output · D5 Context & Reliability · D1 Agentic Architecture
scenarios.brief: A logistics company extracts invoices and bills of lading, about 22,000 documents a month across roughly 50 vendor layouts; some arrive as OCR'd faxes. Claude returns fields through a tool whose JSON schema is strict (vendor, invoice and PO numbers, line items, totals, currency, Incoterm), a validation-retry loop handles failures, and an agent posts results to the ERP. Six vendors supply most of the volume.

questions.trap: More context or reasoning instead of structure
questions.question: The generator targets uncovered branches in the payments module. Last sprint it lifted line coverage from 64% to 89%, and every new test runs green. A reviewer read 40 of them and found one habit in nearly all: call the function, then check that the result is not null or that nothing was thrown. Their names, layout and fixtures match the repository's table-driven style. The prompt's only guidance on quality is the line "write thorough unit tests for each uncovered branch". Which change is the most effective?

options.t: Add three finished tests from the repository to the prompt, each pinning an exact expected value for a named input.
options.why: Runner-up. Few-shot examples are the strongest tool when written rules exist but output still varies. Here there are no rules at all, and the weak habit is uniform, so the first job is to say what a real assertion is.

options.t: Replace the quality line with testable rules: assert an exact output for a stated input, and fail if the branch condition flips.
options.why: Correct. "Thorough" gives the model nothing to check itself against. Categorical rules define a sufficient assertion, including the case a weak test misses (the inverted branch).

options.t: Pass each generated test to a separate Claude instance, without the generator's reasoning, for review before commit.
options.why: Incorrect. An independent reviewer is good for catching subtle errors, but it would judge against the same undefined idea of "thorough". It checks output; it does not define quality.

options.t: Generate tests one source file at a time, then run a separate cross-file pass over the generated tests as a set.
options.why: Incorrect. Per-file plus integration passes fix attention dilution and contradictions across files. The weak assertions appear inside single tests, so splitting the work does not touch them.

questions.explanation: Vague quality words such as "thorough" do not change behaviour; categorical criteria do. Define what counts first, then use examples when defined criteria are applied inconsistently.
questions.decider: The prompt contains no definition of a good assertion and the weak habit is uniform, not inconsistent; if written criteria already existed and output still varied, examples would be the better fix.

eli5.question: The generated tests run green but check almost nothing. The clue is: the prompt's only guidance on quality is the single word "thorough". The tidy coverage numbers are a distraction; the question is what the model was told a good test looks like.
eli5.answer: Think of asking a new cook to make the soup "tasty". You get soup, but nobody said how much salt. The cook needs a recipe card with measurable rules (explicit criteria). Here the rule is: each test checks an exact answer for a named input, and would fail if the branch's logic were flipped. Rule: replace vague quality words with rules you could check.
options: Runner-up. Showing good tests (few-shot examples) helps when rules exist but are applied unevenly. Here there are no rules yet, and the weak habit is the same everywhere.
Correct. It turns "thorough" into rules a test can pass or fail.
A second checker (independent review) would judge against the same vague word. It checks; it does not define good.
Splitting the work per file (multi-pass review) fixes overload across many files. The weakness here sits inside each single test.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think examples are the cure for any weak output. Examples are the cure when the rules are known but applied unevenly. Here the output is uniformly weak and the only rule is the word "thorough". The model did exactly what it was told; nobody told it what a real assertion is. Define the standard before you demonstrate it.

questions.question: Generated tests now assert real values, but their shape varies from run to run. About half use the repository's table-driven layout with a shared fixture; the rest write one function per case and rebuild the fixture each time. Reviewers say the mixed shapes make diffs slow to read. The testing-standards section describes the table-driven layout in two paragraphs, and the job's /memory output lists that file among the loaded memory. What is the most effective change?

options.t: Move the testing conventions into a .claude/rules/ file whose paths: glob matches the test files.
options.why: Runner-up. Path-scoped rules are the right home for conventions that cover files across directories. They would win if the standards were not reaching the job; /memory shows they already load.

options.t: Expand the standards section into a numbered checklist that covers case tables, fixture scope and test naming.
options.why: Incorrect. Explicit criteria help when the rule is vague, but this convention is already described in prose and still applied inconsistently. More prose is more of the same channel.

options.t: Put two or three finished tests copied from the codebase into the generation prompt as models of the form.
options.why: Correct. When instructions alone produce inconsistent output, concrete examples are the most reliable way to show a structural convention.

options.t: Run a PostToolUse hook that rewrites each generated test file into the house layout before it is saved.
options.why: Incorrect. Hooks are good for deterministic normalisation of formats. Turning one-function-per-case into a table-driven test is a design change, not a mechanical one.

questions.explanation: Few-shot examples are the most effective technique when instructions alone give inconsistent output, and they carry structure that prose describes poorly. First check that the instructions load at all; then show, don't tell.
questions.decider: The /memory output shows the standards are already loaded, so the problem is inconsistent application, not delivery; if the file were missing from the job's memory, path-scoped rules would be the fix.

eli5.question: Tests now check real values, but half are shaped one way and half another. The clue is: /memory shows the standards file is already loaded. So the rules are arriving; the model just doesn't apply them evenly.
eli5.answer: A new hire has read the style handbook, yet half their reports look different. Two finished reports from the files would fix it faster than another chapter. Showing finished samples is few-shot prompting, and it carries shape far better than prose. Rule: if written rules arrive but output still varies, show examples.
options: Runner-up. Rules that load by file pattern (path-scoped rules) fix rules that never reach the job. /memory shows they already arrive.
A longer checklist is more of the same prose that is already being followed unevenly.
Correct. Real tests from the codebase show the house shape directly.
An automatic rewrite step (hook) can tidy formats, but it cannot turn separate test functions into a table-driven test.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think inconsistent output means the rules are not reaching the model, so you fix where the rules live. Sometimes that is true. But here the job's memory listing shows the standards are loaded. When rules arrive and are still applied unevenly, the channel is the problem: prose describes a shape poorly. Examples show it.

questions.question: The security dashboard ingests review findings in a fixed shape: severity from a four-value enum, a nullable cwe_id, file, line and description. The review step runs claude -p with --output-format json, and a Python adapter maps whatever keys come back onto that shape. About once a month the adapter breaks when a key is renamed, for example location instead of file. The review blocks merging and already uses about three of its five minutes. Which change best removes the renamed-key failures?

options.t: Pass the dashboard's schema to the CLI with --json-schema and drop the key-mapping adapter from the step.
options.why: Correct. The keys drift because the output shape is unconstrained and reconciled afterwards. Constraining the run to the consumer's schema removes the step that drifts.

options.t: Validate each result against the dashboard schema and rerun the review with the validation errors appended on failure.
options.why: Runner-up. Retry with error feedback is a sound loop for format errors. On a blocking check already at three of five minutes, a second full run breaks the budget; with time to spare it would be a reasonable safety net.

options.t: Add the five field names and the severity values to the review criteria in the repository's CLAUDE.md.
options.why: Incorrect. CLAUDE.md is the right place for review criteria, but describing a shape in instructions is a tendency, not a constraint. Monthly drift is what a tendency looks like at this volume.

options.t: Version the adapter's field mapping and add a contract test that fails the build when the output keys change.
options.why: Incorrect. Good engineering that turns silent breakage into a loud one. It detects the drift after it happens instead of removing it.

questions.explanation: --output-format json gives valid JSON; --json-schema gives your JSON. When a consumer has a fixed contract, enforce it at generation instead of repairing output afterwards.
questions.decider: The review is blocking and already uses three of its five minutes, so a validate-and-rerun loop cannot afford a second run; with no latency limit, retry with feedback would be a reasonable alternative.

eli5.question: A dashboard needs findings in a fixed shape, and once a month a key name drifts and breaks the adapter. The clue is: the review is blocking and already uses three of its five minutes. So any fix that needs a second full run is too slow.
eli5.answer: Think of a form with labelled boxes versus a blank page. On a blank page people write things in any order, and a clerk copies them over, sometimes wrongly. Give them the form and the clerk isn't needed. --json-schema is the form: the CLI produces output in your shape (schema-constrained output). Rule: if a consumer needs a fixed shape, constrain the output, don't repair it.
options: Correct. The run is held to the dashboard's shape, so there is nothing left to map.
Runner-up. Checking and re-asking with the error (retry with feedback) is sound. But a second run won't fit in a five-minute blocking check that already uses three.
Writing the shape in CLAUDE.md is a request, not a constraint. Monthly drift is what a request looks like at volume.
A contract test catches the drift loudly, but only after it happens. The build still breaks.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a validate-and-retry loop is the reliable way to get structured output. It is a good loop, and the exam guide recommends it. But it costs a whole extra run each time it fires, and it reduces failures rather than removing them. When the CLI can constrain output to a schema at generation time, there is nothing to retry.

questions.question: A new CI step runs the nightly debt sweep with claude -p. It finishes in about 20 seconds and posts a well-formed, empty findings array every night. An engineer running the same prompt on her laptop gets around forty findings. In the CI log, the last model turn is a request to run rg across the repository through Bash; the next line is the final empty result, and the job exits with status 0. The sweep's criteria were drafted by that engineer. What is the most likely cause?

options.t: The sweep's criteria live in the engineer's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which the CI runner does not have.
options.why: Runner-up. User-level memory is not shared through the repository, and that would make CI results differ. But missing criteria would change what gets flagged after a search runs; the log shows the run stopping at the search request itself.

options.t: The runner's shallow clone omits the git history the sweep reads, leaving the analysis nothing to compare against.
options.why: Incorrect. Shallow clones cause real CI bugs, but the working tree is still present and rg searches files, not history.

options.t: The --print flag ends the session after the model's first turn, before any requested tool call is run.
options.why: Incorrect. -p selects non-interactive mode; the agentic loop still runs tool calls. That is why it is the standard way to run Claude Code in CI.

options.t: The CI run has no permission rule allowing that Bash search, and a headless session has nobody to approve it.
options.why: Correct. A non-interactive run cannot ask for approval, so an unpermitted tool is unavailable. Fast, error-free, empty output right after a tool request is the signature.

questions.explanation: Headless runs cannot prompt. Every tool a CI workload needs must be allowed up front, or the run quietly does nothing. That is different from the hang you get when non-interactive mode is missing.
questions.decider: The log shows the run ending at the Bash request with no tool output, which points to a denied tool; if the search had run and returned matches but nothing was flagged, missing user-level criteria would be the better explanation.

eli5.question: A CI sweep finishes fast with zero findings, while the same prompt on a laptop finds forty. The clue is: the log ends right after the model asks to run a search through Bash, with no result. The note that the engineer wrote the criteria is a decoy.
eli5.answer: Picture a contractor working alone overnight. He needs a key to the store room, but nobody is there to hand it over. He writes "nothing found" and goes home. A CI run with -p (non-interactive mode) can't ask anyone to approve a tool. If the tool isn't allowed in advance, the run gets nothing. Rule: headless runs can't ask; allow every tool they need up front.
options: Runner-up. Personal settings (user-level CLAUDE.md) aren't on the CI runner, which would change results. But the run stops at the search request itself, before any criteria matter.
A shallow copy of the repository still has all the files. A text search reads files, not history.
-p runs the full loop, tool calls included. It doesn't stop after one turn.
Correct. The search was never permitted, and a headless run has nobody to approve it.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think CI differs from a laptop because some config file is missing. That is often true, and personal memory files really don't travel. But read where the run stops. It stops right at the first tool request, with no output and no error. That is the signature of a denied tool in a session that cannot ask for approval.

questions.question: Review precision is estimated at 78%. Developers dismiss about a fifth of findings with a one-click button that stores only a timestamp, and nobody can say which kinds of finding draw the dismissals. Once a quarter a staff engineer reads 60 dismissed comments and guesses at the noisiest categories. The team wants a per-category false-positive figure that refreshes daily, with no one reading findings by hand, to decide which review criteria to rewrite. Which two changes, together, achieve this? Select TWO

options.t: Add a detected_pattern field to the findings schema that names the review rule behind each finding.
options.why: Correct. Without a rule label, every dismissal is an anecdote. Tagging findings at generation time makes "which categories are wrong" a query.

options.t: Draw a weekly stratified sample of findings per category and have a reviewer label each one as valid or not.
options.why: Runner-up. Stratified sampling is the right way to measure precision per category. It would win if a person could label findings each week; the goal rules out reading by hand.

options.t: Log each dismissal click with the finding's ID to a table that can be joined to the stored findings.
options.why: Correct. The label only helps if the outcome is captured against it. Joined together, they give per-pattern dismissal rates that update by themselves.

options.t: Route dismissed findings to a separate Claude instance that labels each one as a true or false positive.
options.why: Incorrect. An independent instance is useful for review, but here it adds a second opinion without supplying categories. It also depends on dismissals being recorded first.

options.t: Add an optional free-text box to the dismiss button asking developers to explain why the finding was wrong.
options.why: Incorrect. Optional free text is filled in rarely and worded differently every time. It creates another pile for someone to read by hand.

questions.explanation: To improve precision you need to know which rule produced each finding and what happened to it. A detected_pattern field plus dismissals recorded against it turns developer behaviour into a per-pattern signal.
questions.decider: The team wants the figure without anyone reading findings by hand; if a weekly human labelling budget existed, stratified sampling per category would be a strong second choice.

eli5.question: The team wants to know, daily and automatically, which kinds of finding developers reject. The clue is: "with no one reading findings by hand". That rules out any plan that relies on a person labelling findings.
eli5.answer: Imagine a shop that wants to know which products get returned. Each item needs a product code on it, and each return needs to be logged against that code. Then a report counts returns per product by itself. Here the product code is a detected_pattern field, and the return log is the dismissal record. Rule: tag each finding with its rule, and record what happened to it.
options: Correct. Each finding carries the rule that produced it.
Runner-up. A sample drawn per category (stratified sampling) is the right way to measure precision, but someone has to read it. The goal says nobody reads by hand.
Correct. Dismissals are recorded against each finding, so they can be counted per rule.
A second model (independent instance) gives an opinion but no categories. It also needs to know which findings were dismissed.
Optional free text is rarely filled in, and creates another pile someone has to read.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think measuring precision always means labelling a sample. Sampling is the right tool when a person can label. But the goal here is a figure that refreshes daily with no one reading. Developers already judge every finding by clicking dismiss. Capture that judgement and the category it applies to, and the measurement runs itself.

questions.question: The nightly sweep now uses the Message Batches API: one request per file, 2,400 requests a night. A script walks the result list and attaches the nth result to the nth file submitted. This week a developer found a comment about SQL string-building posted on a YAML config file. Last night 39 requests came back errored, and the script responds to any failure by resubmitting the full batch. Which change best fixes the sweep's result handling?

options.t: Have the model repeat the file path as a field in each response, and match results to files on that field.
options.why: Runner-up. Echoing an identifier in the output does fix pairing for successful results. An errored request returns no model output, so the 39 failures could not be identified for resubmission.

options.t: Set each request's custom_id to its file path, then pair results and resubmit failed requests by that ID.
options.why: Correct. Batch results are not returned in submission order; custom_id is the field built for correlation, and it also identifies exactly which requests to resend.

options.t: Submit the files as twenty-four batches of 100 requests and pair results by position within each smaller batch.
options.why: Incorrect. Smaller batches do not change the ordering semantics. Positional pairing is wrong at any batch size.

options.t: Move the sweep to synchronous calls from a worker pool, writing each response beside its file as it returns.
options.why: Incorrect. It fixes pairing but gives up the 50% batch discount on a workload that is cost-sensitive and has all night.

questions.explanation: Batch results arrive in any order; correlate by custom_id, never by position. Resubmit only the failed requests by their custom_id, which keeps the cost saving.
questions.decider: 39 requests errored and an errored request returns no model output, so a path echoed in the response cannot identify them; if no request ever failed, matching on an echoed path would work for pairing.

eli5.question: Batch results are being matched to files by their position, and a finding landed on the wrong file. The clue is: 39 requests came back as errors. An error has no model answer in it, which matters for one of the options.
eli5.answer: Think of sending 2,400 parcels and getting the receipts back in a heap. Counting down the heap doesn't tell you which receipt is whose. You need a reference number on each parcel. In the Batches API that reference is custom_id: it comes back with every result, including failures. Rule: match batch results by custom_id, never by position, and resend only the failures.
options: Runner-up. Asking the model to repeat the file path works for answers that come back. An errored request has no answer, so you can't tell which 39 to resend.
Correct. The ID comes back on every result, success or error.
Smaller batches still don't promise order. Matching by position is wrong at any size.
Live calls fix the matching but lose the batch discount on a cost-sensitive nightly job.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think any unique key will do for matching results, so having the model repeat the file path seems as good as an ID. It works for successes. But an errored request returns no model output at all. Only a key attached to the request itself survives failure. That is what custom_id is.

questions.question: The review procedure (criteria, severity definitions, output schema and exclusions) is a 300-line prompt pasted into three places: the Actions workflow, a pre-push script and a wiki page. The copies now disagree on two severity thresholds. Developers also start the review by hand from inside their working Claude Code sessions, and its long file-by-file reasoning then fills the conversation they were using to make the change. Where should the procedure live?

options.t: Save it as a project slash command in .claude/commands/ and have the workflow and script invoke it.
options.why: Runner-up. A project command is shared and versioned, which ends the drift. It would win if the review ran only in CI; run from a working session, its output lands in that session's context.

options.t: Move it into the repository's root CLAUDE.md under a Review heading, loaded in every session and run.
options.why: Incorrect. CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded, universal standards. A 300-line on-demand procedure would weigh on every unrelated session.

options.t: Place it in a .claude/rules/ file whose paths: glob covers the source tree it reviews.
options.why: Incorrect. Path-scoped rules load conventions while matching files are edited. A review is a task you invoke, not a convention to load.

options.t: Define a project skill in .claude/skills/ with context: fork in its frontmatter, invoked by name.
options.why: Correct. One versioned definition ends the drift, and context: fork runs it in an isolated sub-agent context, so the long reasoning stays out of the developer's conversation.

questions.explanation: Skills are on-demand workflows and can run isolated with context: fork; CLAUDE.md holds always-loaded standards. One versioned definition invoked by name stops copies from diverging.

questions.question: Results post to the ERP through a post_invoice tool the agent calls once it is satisfied with a document. Policy says any invoice over $50,000 must be approved by a person before posting. options.why: Incorrect. Criteria and examples improve the agent's judgment, but compliance stays probabilistic. The failures happened exactly in the case the examples would show.

questions.decider: The agent itself decides when to call post_invoice, so anything it must choose to honour can be skipped; if the posting code read the flag, a PostToolUse flag would also enforce the rule.

options.why: Runner-up. Stratified sampling is the right way to measure error rates by field and vendor. It measures after posting; it does not stop an individual wrong value from reaching the ERP.

options.t: Score confidence per field, calibrate it on a labelled set, and queue documents with any field below its threshold.

options.why: Correct. Well-formed errors can only be caught against an outside source of truth. A CAD vendor in the master contradicts a USD extraction with no human involved.

options.t: Extract every document twice with different prompts and queue it only when the two outputs disagree on a field.
options.why: Incorrect. Agreement is another proxy: a systematically misread layout gives the same wrong value both times.

questions.explanation: Self-reported confidence and cross-run agreement are proxies, not measures. Well-formed but wrong values are caught by something outside the extraction: calibrated per-field confidence for routing and independent business records for verification.
